pages.text: Once upon a time, three little pigs left their mother's house to build homes of their own.
The first pig was lazy and quickly built his house out of straw.
The second pig was also in a hurry and built his house out of sticks.
The third pig worked slowly and carefully, building a strong house of bricks.
One day, a big hungry wolf came prowling through the forest.
The wolf knocked on the straw door and called, "Little pig, little pig, let me come in!"
"Not by the hair of my chinny-chin-chin!" answered the pig from inside.
"Then I'll huff, and I'll puff, and I'll blow your house in!" growled the wolf.
The wolf huffed and puffed with all his might, and the straw house fell right down.
The first pig ran as fast as he could to his brother's stick house.
The wolf knocked again: "Little pigs, little pigs, let me come in!"
The pigs refused, and the wolf huffed and puffed until the stick house tumbled down too.
Both pigs dashed off, frightened, to their brother's strong brick house.
The wolf demanded to be let in, but all three pigs shouted "No!" together.
The wolf huffed and puffed with every bit of strength he had, but the brick house did not budge.
Furious, the wolf climbed onto the roof to sneak down the chimney, and landed straight in a pot of hot water.
Yelping in surprise, the wolf ran off into the forest and was never seen again.
The three little pigs learned that careful, patient work always keeps you safe in the end.
A little girl always wore a warm red hooded cloak, so everyone called her Little Red Riding Hood.
One day, her mother said, "Take this basket of cakes to your grandmother, for she is unwell."
"Stay on the path and do not talk to strangers," her mother warned kindly.
The girl walked alone along the trail through the big, shadowy forest.
A clever wolf appeared and asked, "Where are you going with that basket, little girl?"
"To my grandmother's house, just past those tall trees," she answered, trusting him.
The wolf dashed off down a shortcut and reached grandma's cottage first.
He locked grandma safely in the closet and put on her nightcap and gown.
When Little Red Riding Hood knocked, the wolf called out in a thin voice, "Come in, dear."
"Grandmother, what big ears you have!" she said, feeling puzzled.
"All the better to hear you with," said the wolf, pulling the blanket to his chin.
"Grandmother, what big eyes you have!" she went on, growing more uneasy.
"All the better to see you with," said the wolf, sitting up slowly.
"Grandmother, what big teeth you have!" she cried, stepping back.
"All the better to... hug you with!" shouted the wolf, leaping up from the bed.
She ran out screaming, and a woodcutter working nearby heard the commotion.
The woodcutter rushed in and chased the startled wolf far away from the house.
They found grandma safe and sound, hidden in the closet.
Everyone sat down together and shared the cakes, grateful and happy to be safe.
Little Red Riding Hood learned to never again linger and talk with strangers in the forest.
A very fast hare loved to tease the tortoise for being so slow.
"You'll never get anywhere at that pace!" the hare laughed every single day.
Tired of the jokes, the tortoise said, "Then let's have a race, and we shall see."
The hare laughed even louder, but happily agreed to the challenge.
All the forest animals gathered to watch, with the owl and the fox as judges.
"Ready, set, go!" called the fox, and the race began.
The hare shot off like an arrow and was soon far, far ahead.
Glancing back and seeing the tortoise so far behind, he laughed, "I have plenty of time!"
So sure of winning, the hare decided to rest a while under a shady tree.
He closed his eyes just to rest his legs, and soon fell fast asleep.
The tortoise, slow but steady, kept walking one careful step at a time.
He passed right by the sleeping hare, quiet as could be, and carried on.
As the sun began to set, the tortoise drew closer and closer to the finish line.
Suddenly, the hare woke with a start and looked around in confusion.
He ran as fast as his legs would carry him, but the finish line was already in sight ahead.
The tortoise crossed the line first, to cheers and applause from all the animals.
The hare arrived out of breath and embarrassed, but shook the tortoise's paw with a warm smile.
Everyone learned that slow and steady, with patience, wins the race.
A little girl with golden hair, named Goldilocks, wandered alone through the forest.
She found a cosy little house, and since the door stood open, she stepped inside to look around.
The house belonged to three bears: Papa Bear, Mama Bear, and Baby Bear.
On the table sat three bowls of porridge, still steaming warm.
She tasted the first bowl, Papa Bear's, but it was much too hot.
She tasted the second, Mama Bear's, but it was much too cold.
The third, Baby Bear's, was just right, and she ate every last spoonful.
Next she tried Papa Bear's big chair, but it was much too hard.
She tried Mama Bear's chair, but it was much too soft.
Baby Bear's little chair was just right, but it broke the moment she sat down.
Tired from her long walk, she went upstairs and found three beds in a row.
Papa Bear's bed was much too hard, and Mama Bear's was much too soft.
Baby Bear's little bed was just right, and she fell fast asleep right away.
Soon after, the three bears came home, hungry from their morning walk.
"Someone's been eating my porridge!" said Papa Bear in his great big voice.
"And someone broke my chair!" whimpered Baby Bear, staring at the pieces.
They went upstairs and found Goldilocks fast asleep in Baby Bear's bed.
She woke up startled to see the three bears staring at her, said a quick sorry, and ran straight out the door.
Goldilocks learned that it's always best to ask before entering someone else's home.
In the hot summer sun, a hardworking ant gathered food every single day without rest.
Nearby, a grasshopper spent his days singing, dancing, and playing his little fiddle.
"Come and play with me!" the grasshopper called, lounging carefree in the sunshine.
"I can't, I must store food for winter," the ant replied, never pausing her work.
The grasshopper laughed, "Winter is so far away! Why worry so much?"
Day after day, the ant kept carrying tiny grains back to her safe little burrow.
Slowly, the leaves began to fall and the wind turned cold and sharp.
Autumn passed quickly, and one morning the first snow blanketed the whole forest.
With no food stored away at all, the grasshopper felt the cold and hunger creep in.
Shivering, he knocked on the ant's door, feeling ashamed and afraid to ask.
The ant opened the door and saw her friend, sad and trembling with cold.
Without hesitation, she welcomed him in and warmed him by her cosy little fire.
Kindly, she shared the grains she had carefully saved all through the summer.
The grasshopper thanked her warmly and promised to plan ahead from that day on.
They spent the rest of winter together, telling stories by the fireside.
The following spring, the two friends worked side by side, happier than ever.
They learned that planning ahead, and helping one another, always makes life better.
An old woman baked a sweet gingerbread man and set him in the oven to bake.
When she opened the oven door, he suddenly jumped out and started to run.
"Run, run, as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the Gingerbread Man!" he shouted.
The old woman chased him around the kitchen, but he was far too quick.
Down the road, a dog tried to catch him, but he sang his little rhyme and kept on running.
A cow grazing nearby tried too, but could never quite catch up.
A horse in the field neighed and galloped after him, but the gingerbread man was too swift.
At last he reached a wide, rushing river and did not know how to cross.
A clever fox appeared and said, "Climb onto my back, and I'll carry you across."
The gingerbread man, a little unsure but with no other choice, climbed on.
The fox swam slowly, saying the water was getting deeper and deeper.
"Climb onto my neck, so you don't get wet," she said, and he climbed higher.
A little further on, she warned, "Climb onto my nose, or you'll get soaked!"
The moment he reached her nose, the fox opened her mouth with a quick snap.
In that instant, the Gingerbread Man realized, too late, that the fox was far too clever to trust.
The tale of the Gingerbread Man was told for years after, and everyone learned to be wary of strangers who seem a little too helpful.
Little Sara was always afraid to speak in front of the class.
Her hands would shake whenever she had to present a project.
Sara's grandmother gave her a small round golden mirror.
"This mirror always shows someone brave," grandma said with a smile.
Sara looked into the mirror and saw only her own face.
"But I only see myself," Sara said, puzzled by the answer.
"Exactly," grandma replied. "Courage already lives inside you."
The next day, Sara carried the mirror hidden in her pocket.
Before speaking, she quickly glanced at her brave reflection.
She took a deep breath, smiled, and began to speak slowly and clearly.
The class clapped, and Sara's heart filled with pride.
Sara learned that courage doesn't come from outside, but from within.
In the neighborhood lived Tom, a boy full of good ideas.
One day he saw an elderly neighbor struggling with heavy bags.
Tom ran over and helped carry the bags to her door.
The neighbor smiled and thanked him with a slice of homemade cake.
Tom realized that helping others made him feel truly happy.
He decided to start a club with friends to help the neighborhood.
They made a colorful poster and called it the Helping Hands Club.
Every week, the group helped someone different around the neighborhood.
They watered plants, walked dogs, and helped tidy the park.
The neighbors began to smile more and talk to each other more.
The neighborhood became a friendlier place thanks to the little club.
Tom learned that small acts of help can change the world around us.
Little Nuno was always very busy, running from place to place.
He rushed to school, to games, and to his friends' houses.
But Nuno began to feel more and more tired and a little confused.
His grandfather noticed and invited him to sit together in the garden.
"Close your eyes and listen," grandpa said in a soft voice.
Nuno heard the birds singing and the wind moving through the leaves.
Then grandpa asked, "What do you feel, right now?"
Nuno thought for a moment and said, "I feel tired, but also calm."
"That is your inner voice," grandpa explained gently.
"It always knows what you need, if you stop to listen."
From that day on, Nuno paused every afternoon to breathe quietly.
He learned that knowing his own feelings helped him feel happier.
Little Iris thought she was too young to help anyone at all.
One day, her grandfather gave her a small bag of sunflower seeds.
"Plant a seed every time you do something kind," he said.
Iris helped a classmate pick up the pencils that had fallen.
That afternoon, she planted her very first seed in the little garden.
The next day, she helped set the table without being asked.
She planted another seed and smiled watching the garden grow.
Weeks passed, and Iris kept doing small, kind little gestures.
She helped neighbors, shared toys, and listened to sad friends.
The garden filled up with tall sunflowers shining in the sun.
Iris's friends also began to be kinder to one another.
Iris realized that kindness, like seeds, grows when it is shared.
